vignette:
Mariana was thirty-six when the assault happened-a guest at the hotel she managed, a man with a confident smile who had checked in for a business conference. She had walked him to his room, a courtesy she offered to VIPs, and he had pulled her inside before she could react. The memory was not a story she could tell, even to herself. She knew what had happened, but when she tried to find words for it, the language evaporated, replaced by a thick, physical shame that settled in her chest. That shame came back every time she recalled the event, and with it came a conviction that something was profoundly wrong with her-that the assault had happened because of the sort of person she was, because of some flaw she carried. The shame and the self-blame made the memory harder to hold, more fragmented, like trying to grip smoke. She could not piece together a coherent sequence; the beginning and end were missing, and only the worst fragments-the feel of the door clicking shut, the pressure of his hand-remained.

In the months that followed, Mariana threw herself into her work. She arrived before dawn and stayed until the lobby was empty, taking on projects no one else wanted, rewriting shift schedules, inspecting every corner of the property. The overwork was not ambition; it was a way to keep her mind occupied, to prevent the intrusive images from surfacing. When she was exhausted, she could not think. But the strategy backfired: the longer she avoided the memory, the more disordered it became, and the more her body kept reacting-her heart pounding at a sudden knock, her muscles tensing when a male guest laughed in a certain tone. She had come to believe that her body was an enemy, betraying her with fear responses that made no sense in safe situations. That belief drove her to avoid any man who vaguely resembled the guest: a similar build, the same shade of brown hair, a certain gait. She would ask a female colleague to handle those check-ins, inventing excuses. Each avoidance confirmed, in a quiet way, that she was too broken to function normally.

During quiet moments in her office, Mariana found herself ruminating about revenge. She imagined confronting him, exposing him, causing him harm. The fantasies provided a fleeting sense of control, but they also deepened her conviction that she was defective-that a decent person would not spend hours plotting retaliation. The rumination, in turn, made the memory feel more vivid and more shameful, because she could see herself in a violent light. It was a loop she could sense but could not name: she avoided the memory by overworking, which led to more rumination, which cemented her belief that the assault defined her character. She began to think that if only she could get even, she could restore something lost, but the thought itself made her feel monstrous.

Her relationship suffered. Her partner, Carlos, noticed she was distant, always tired, quick to anger when he approached her from behind. She could not explain why; the words would not come. What she could say was that she needed space, and he gave it, but the distance only reinforced her sense of being fundamentally wrong. Eventually, a panic attack during a routine staff meeting-triggered by a guest walking past the conference room who had the same cologne as the assailant-convinced her that she could not manage this alone. She scheduled an appointment with a therapist, terrified that the therapist would confirm what she already believed: that the damage was permanent. But a part of her, small and stubborn, hoped that perhaps there was another way to understand what had happened, a story she could finally piece together without the weight of shame.
